concepts.name: Convolution
concepts.summary: A small window of weights (a kernel) slid across a signal; at each stop it multiplies the values beneath it by the kernel weights and sums them to one output number, then steps over. Example: signal [1,2,3,4,5] with kernel [1,0,-1] gives 1·1+0·2−1·3 = −2 at the first stop, marching down the line to [−2,−2,−2]. Each output is a dot product of the kernel with the local window it covers. (Upstairs: the same operation, at scale, is how image- and video-processing engines slide learned kernels.)

concepts.name: The Receptive Field
concepts.summary: Each convolution output depends only on the small local neighbourhood of the input beneath the kernel at that stop, its receptive field, not on the whole signal. Sliding the identical kernel across every position means one small set of weights is reused everywhere: weight sharing. A width-k kernel uses only k weights no matter how long the signal is.

concepts.name: 1-D, 2-D, 3-D Kernels
concepts.summary: The same convolution works on any number of axes: a 1-D kernel is a strip sliding along a line (summing over k values); a 2-D kernel is a square patch sliding over a grid of rows and columns (summing over a small area, e.g. 3×3); a 3-D kernel is a box sliding over a volume along three axes at once (summing over a small box, e.g. 3×3×3). Same multiply-and-sum, more directions of travel.
